beats.script_body: This is where New York City—then New Amsterdam—was born. The area packs the same historic punch as colonial sections of Boston and Philadelphia. It was on Wall Street that George Washington took the oath of office as America's first president, and it was here, at Fraunces Tavern, that the Sons of Liberty gathered to plot the overthrow of the British. At Castle Clinton and then Ellis Island, millions of immigrants flooded the city in the 19th and 20th centuries to get their first glimpse of a “promised land.”

As recent history has overshadowed other sights, for many visitors this has simply become the place to pay respects at the 9/11 Memorial and Museum.

It's a truly transporting area, and one that has been voraciously swallowing up other neighborhoods—Little Italy and the Jewish Lower East Side—for the past few decades.

There are a handful of worthwhile places to shop for Italian food, eat gelato, or get Italian coffee, but very few real Italian Americans around anymore.

name: Lower East Side

beats.script_body: For millions, this area was once the portal to America. The buildings you see on the Lower East Side were built expressly to house the teeming masses of immigrants who flooded into New York between roughly 1840 and 1930. At the turn of the last century, this was the most densely populated area in the world, with a dozen people to an apartment and pushcarts jamming the streets. Some remnants of that life survive in the old-world fabric and luggage stores along Orchard Street.

beats.script_body: For 25 years, the non-profit Big Apple Greeter has paired volunteer New Yorkers with visitors for free, highly personal looks at the city. The guides aren't expected to spout history or architecture; instead they introduce tourists to the city they know and love, taking them to areas few outsiders see. The four-hour tours are for individuals and couples—the largest group accepted is five—and are so hugely popular that you should book four weeks in advance, because many would-be participants are turned away.

beats.source_passage: If you’d like to tour a specific neighborhood with an expert guide, contact Big Apple Greeter (www.bigapplegreeter.org; 212/669-8159). For 25 years this non-profit group has been pairing volunteers with visitors for free and highly personal looks at the city. The guides are not expected to be able to spout history or talk in detail about the architecture of the places you’ll be visiting. Instead, they introduce tourists to the city they know and love deeply, taking them to areas that few outsiders see. The 4-hour tours are for individuals and couples (the largest group they accept is five people) and are hugely popular, so book 4 weeks in advance of arrival (or more), because many would-be participants are turned away.

beats.script_body: Greenwich Village has always been where the city's outsiders and oddballs found a haven. In Dutch Colonial times it was farmland set outside the walls of the city. At the turn of the 20th century it was a bohemian enclave where artists of all sorts—Mark Twain, Edgar Allan Poe, Eugene O'Neill, and Winslow Homer among them—could find cheap lodging and companionship. In the 1950s it sat at the center of the Beat movement; in the '60s and '70s the area around Christopher Street became the hub of a burgeoning gay rights movement; and in the '80s it was a hotbed of AIDS-related activism.

name: Meatpacking District

The book calls it NYC's adult Disneyland, filled with late-night clubs, bars, and restaurants that are unhindered by the city's zoning laws—since there are no schools or churches in this part of town.

beats.script_body: Manhattan's Chelsea neighborhood is today what SoHo was 10 years ago, and what Greenwich Village was 20 years ago—meaning that if you want to go art gallery hopping, this is where to head. Three final reasons to come: the Whitney Museum, the High Line park (a marvel of urban reclamation), and Little Island, a custom-built pleasure isle in the Hudson.

name: Flatiron District

beats.script_body: As you meander through these areas you're likely to see brown street signs proclaiming “Ladies Mile.” It was on this stretch, mostly on Broadway and Park Avenue South, that the first wave of department stores transformed the lives of New Yorkers in the 1850s. Instead of hopping from a dry-goods shop for fabric to a milliner for hats to a cobbler for shoes, women came from all over the city to outfit themselves and their homes in stores that had everything under one roof. Notice the large plate-glass windows on many facades, another department store innovation.

name: Gramercy Park

beats.script_body: Gramercy Park is named for the only privately owned park in the city—the keys go to those apartment owners whose windows overlook the park. Around it, beautifully preserved historic homes and clubs include the wisteria-clad home of former Mayor James Harper at 4 Gramercy Park South, the Players Club at number 16 (whose members included Edwin Booth and Mark Twain), and the National Arts Club at number 15, a hangout for Woodrow Wilson and Theodore Dreiser.

name: Midtown West

beats.script_body: Midtown West encompasses several famous places: Madison Square Garden, the Garment District, Rockefeller Center, the Theater District, and Times Square. It's the area most people picture when they think of New York, and the reason so many visitors say, “It's a nice place to visit, but I couldn't ever live there.” Basing their judgment on crowded, loud, pushy midtown, they're absolutely right—which is why so few New Yorkers actually live here. In certain parts there's no residential housing whatsoever.

beats.source_passage: Midtown West, a vast area, encompasses several famous places: Madison Square Garden, the Garment District, Rockefeller Center, the Theater District, and Times Square. It’s the area most people think of when they think of New York, and the reason why so many visitors say with a smirk, “Well, it’s a nice place to visit, but I couldn’t ever live there.” And because they’re basing their judgments on crowded, loud, pushy midtown, they’re absolutely right: It’s unlivable . . . which is why so few New Yorkers actually live in this area. In certain parts of midtown there’s no residential housing whatsoever, and it’s only the tourists who attempt to get a good night’s sleep in this bustling neighborhood.

name: Upper East Side

beats.script_body: The zip code 10021 is the richest in the world, and it belongs to the Upper East Side—in particular the swank swath of pavement that runs from 61st to 80th streets. Also known as “The Gold Coast” and “Millionaire's Mile,” this is the stomping ground for New York's high society: the Prada-clad women and old-money men who sit on the boards of the neighborhood museums, go to cocktail parties, and endow scholarships for kicks. Their mansions and marble-faced townhouses make for nifty sightseeing.

name: Upper West Side

beats.script_body: In some ways the Upper West Side has the most suburban vibe of any of Manhattan's neighborhoods. National chain stores line the major thoroughfares and the sidewalks swarm with strollers. It's a popular area for families thanks to its proximity to Central Park, the American Museum of Natural History, and the Children's Museum of Manhattan, and it's home to New York's famous performing arts hub, Lincoln Center.

It’s a popular area for families thanks to its proximity to Central Park, the American Museum of Natural History, and the Children’s Museum of Manhattan. It’s still an extremely pleasant place to visit with good, if chain-oriented, shopping; a handful of top-notch museums; New York’s famous performing arts hub, Lincoln Center; and, of course, access to the glories of Central Park.

beats.script_body: Perhaps the most rapidly transforming neighborhood in the city, Harlem is safer and cleaner than it's been in decades, but may be losing some of its intrinsic character. It has been a largely African-American neighborhood since the 1920s—home to some of the greatest Black writers, politicians, and artists of the 20th century—and is now drawing an increasing number of non-Black residents, lured by lower real estate prices and the beauty of a brownstone-lined community.

beats.script_body: Brooklyn Heights, right off the Brooklyn Bridge, boasts spectacular views of Manhattan and is one of the borough's two most affluent neighborhoods. Filled with lovely Beaux Arts brownstone buildings, it was the first neighborhood in the city to be landmarked. name: Williamsburg

beats.script_body: Williamsburg has a split personality. Part of it houses one of the largest Hasidic Jewish communities in the world; walk the streets peopled by this sect and you may feel as if you've stepped back into an old-country shtetl—an illusion only somewhat ruined by the incongruous but ever-present cellphones. The other half is hipster heaven, a neighborhood of art galleries, bustling boîtes, and soigné boutiques.

name: Queens

beats.script_body: Archie Bunker no longer lives in Queens. The grouchy, bigoted xenophobe at the center of the famed 1970s sitcom All in the Family probably wouldn't recognize the borough today. In just the past 50 years it has gone from a somewhat insulated community of Irish and Italian Americans to the most international community in the United States. A single afternoon can make a visitor feel like a globe-trotter—downing samosas or shopping for saris in very Indian Jackson Heights, breaking plates at a Greek restaurant in Astoria, or buying miracle water and tacos at a Mexican botanica in Corona.

beats.source_passage: Archie Bunker no longer lives in Queens. In fact, the grouchy, bigoted xenophobe at the center of the famed 1970s sitcom All in the Family probably wouldn’t recognize the borough today. In just the past 50 years it’s gone from being a somewhat insulated community of Irish and Italian Americans to the most international community in the United States. A single afternoon in Queens can make a visitor feel like a globe-trotter, which gives Queens a special appeal, despite the dreary, industrial look of much of it. Whether you’re downing samosas or shopping for saris in very Indian Jackson Heights, breaking plates at a Greek restaurant in Astoria, or buying miracle water and tacos at a Mexican botanica in Corona, there’s much to taste, smell, and experience.

name: Manhattan

beats.script_body: Finding your way around Manhattan is easier than in almost any other city because of the careful plan adopted for its avenues and streets. In the areas above 14th Street, the city fathers imposed a strict grid, leveling hills and tearing down existing homes to create straight, evenly spaced thoroughfares in all but a few places. The grid consists of numbered streets and avenues that cross at right angles—so if you can count to 100, you can get around this surprisingly compact island.

beats.source_passage: Finding your way around Manhattan is easier than in almost any other city because of the careful plan that was adopted for laying out the city’s avenues and streets. In the areas above 14th Street, the city fathers imposed a strict grid upon Manhattan, leveling hills and tearing down existing homes to create straight, evenly spaced thoroughfares in all but a few places. The grid consists of numbered streets and avenues that cross each other at right angles. If you can count up to 100, you can get around this surprisingly compact island.
